st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: Harvey accepts the need for realistic, task-specific legal-AI evaluation and materially develops it through LAB’s long-horizon, matter-based assignments, reviewable work products, expert rubrics and strict all-pass grading. It also frames results as guidance for selective delegation and lawyer review rather than proof of autonomous competence, while acknowledging incomplete coverage and deferring performance claims.

kp.k: LAB targets long-horizon legal work rather than isolated reasoning
kp.d: Harvey presents its Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB), announced on 6 May 2026, as an open-source means of evaluating agents on assignments resembling law-firm work. It distinguishes LAB from LegalBench, CUAD, LEXam and Harvey’s earlier BigLaw Bench, which it characterizes as testing short-horizon reasoning. This is Harvey’s account of the benchmark’s purpose and differentiation, not a reported finding that agents can already complete such assignments reliably.
qs: LAB was built to evaluate and improve agent capabilities for supporting real world work done by lawyers.

Existing evaluations, including [LegalBench](https://hazyresearch.stanford.edu/legalbench/), [CUAD](https://www.atticusprojectai.org/cuad/), [LEXam](https://lexam-benchmark.github.io/), and our own earlier work on BigLaw Bench, have graded short-horizon reasoning: read a contract, answer a question, compare cases, or analyze an argument.

kp.k: Assignments model associate work within closed client matters
kp.d: Tasks pair brief partner-style instructions with a closed universe of matter materials and require reviewable legal work product. Instructions average fifty words; environments mix relevant and peripheral files and distribute issues across documents. The benchmark therefore tests context building, document selection and synthesis in open-ended assignments, rather than simply answers to legal questions.
qs: The agent’s instructions are written as a request for work from a partner to an associate.
The client matter defines a closed-universe set of documents and other materials that are needed for the law firm to complete work on behalf of the client.
Instructions are short, averaging just fifty words.
An agent must start from a loose instruction, build context across the matter files, and use that context to produce the relevant deliverables.

kp.k: Deployment framing emphasizes delegation and lawyer review
kp.d: Harvey argues that practice-specific capability measurements could help firms identify tasks suitable for agents, assess AI investment ROI and shift lawyers toward delegation and review. Where agents struggle, it recommends keeping execution heavily human-in-the-loop. These are intended deployment benefits, not measured changes in staffing, leverage ratios or financial returns.
qs: By articulating where agents can do all, some, or none of a task, LAB helps law firms measure the ROI of AI investments and where such investments can augment their teams’ work.

Understanding where agents are capable across practice areas allows firms to identify opportunities to deploy them in order to accelerate client value while moving lawyers to a high-leverage delegate and review pattern.
Identifying areas where agents struggle also allows firms to understand where task execution should remain heavily human-in-the-loop.

kp.k: Expert rubrics operationalize scrutiny of completed work
kp.d: LAB grades final deliverables against expert-written atomic, binary criteria covering substantive and presentation requirements. Criteria are tied to individual deliverable files and are intended to emulate partner or client scrutiny. Harvey says the same criteria can support LLM judging, model and harness comparisons, and training rewards; this describes benchmark grading, rather than evidence that human verification before reliance is unnecessary.
qs: Each rubric breaks down what these stakeholders would scrutinize in a submitted deliverable into atomic, binary pass/fail criteria: facts, conclusions, citations, severity ratings, recommendations, deadlines, dollar amounts, and formatting choices.
Each criterion is tied to a specific deliverable file.
The same criteria can be applied by an LLM judge, used to compare models and harness changes, and fed back into agent training loops as per-criterion reward signals.

kp.k: All-pass grading treats missing issues as material incompleteness
kp.d: A task counts as complete only when every rubric criterion passes. Harvey justifies this stringent standard by arguing that an omitted issue can change deal economics, necessitate rework before closing or cause subsequent problems. Its rejection of partial credit is a methodological position about high-stakes legal deliverables, not an empirical estimate of their usefulness.
qs: Importantly, a task is marked complete only if every criterion passes, a concept we refer to as **all-pass grading**.
A deal-team report that identifies eight of ten risks is not 80% useful; it is materially incomplete.
The missing issue could change deal economics, require the analysis to be redone before closing, or surface as a problem after the deal closes.

kp.k: M&A example tests integrated risk analysis and recommendations
kp.d: The illustrative task concerns the fictional acquisition of Crestview Software Solutions in a $458 million, 100% equity transaction. Agents must examine a data room containing eight material contracts and adjacent materials, identify change-of-control risks and prepare a review-ready memorandum. Its 57 criteria cover nine planted legal issues, including financial exposure, consent timelines and inconsistent contractual definitions. This illustrates task design, not observed agent performance.
qs: As an example, one corporate M&A task asks the agent to analyze change-of-control provisions in connection with the proposed (fictional) acquisition of Crestview Software Solutions in a $458 million, 100% equity transaction.

It must include, amongst other things, an executive summary with a risk mapping, a contract-by-contract analysis of the relevant provisions, severity ratings, and recommendations on how to mitigate each risk identified.
For the change-of-control task, the rubric contains 57 criteria covering nine legal issues planted across the matter.

kp.k: Initial coverage is broad but explicitly incomplete
kp.d: The announcement describes 1,250 tasks across 24 practice areas, with more than 75,000 expert-written criteria. Harvey says task development began with real matters handled by practicing lawyers, broken into assignments normally delegated to associates. The initial scope covers transactional, advisory, regulatory and litigation work, but excludes many practices and task types.
qs: The first version of LAB includes more than 1,200 agent tasks across 24 legal practice areas, and is evaluated by over 75,000 expert-written rubric criteria.
The change-of-control task is one of 1,250 tasks in LAB, spanning 24 legal practice areas.
To scale the benchmark, we started with real client matters handled by practicing lawyers in each practice area.
The 24 practice areas in this release are not exhaustive, and many task types within those areas remain uncovered.

kp.k: Launch deferred scores and submission normalization
kp.d: Harvey intentionally launched without a leaderboard, citing the evolving dataset and a desire for community input on how to communicate performance. It promised baseline results for leading open- and closed-source models and normalized submission guidance in the following weeks. Although the document’s holding note references a separate results post, the supplied text gives no model scores or comparative performance findings.
qs: We're intentionally launching LAB without a leaderboard because we expect the dataset to evolve over time and we want to work with the community to ensure results are clear and intuitive in how they convey agent performance.
Initial results on LAB for leading open and closed-source models will be published in the coming weeks following additional input from research partners and feedback from the community.

This release will also provide guidance for submitting benchmark runs under normalized conditions to allow third-parties to communicate improvements made on any part of the agent stack and to track how scores change as the benchmark evolves with new tasks and other extensions.

kp.k: Open benchmarking is intended to accelerate agent development
kp.d: Harvey argues that public benchmarks can accelerate capabilities as well as measure them, drawing an analogy with coding benchmarks and its engineering team’s experience. It reports early LAB use internally and in research on post-training, memory, legal skills and harness optimization. It seeks lawyer and firm input on task realism and review standards, alongside technical contributions to agent planning, retrieval and tool use.
qs: In coding, agent benchmarks have served as an important leading indicator of agent capability.
A strong public benchmark doesn’t only measure progress, it helps accelerate it.

We are already seeing LAB being used by both our internal teams for product evaluation and the larger research community to explore open-weight post-training, auto-research, memory, domain-specific legal skills, and harness optimizations for long-horizon agent work.

kp.k: Planned expansion includes in-house and adjacent professional work
kp.d: Harvey’s roadmap extends beyond the initial law-firm focus to additional practices, in-house legal work and adjacent professional services, including asset management, banking and tax. It also plans more diverse datasets usable for fine-tuning and training. These are future coverage ambitions rather than capabilities demonstrated by this release.
qs: Expanding coverage to all Biglaw practice areas and coverage of tasks within those practice areas.
Expanding coverage beyond law firms to cover other professional service workflows from in-house counsel, to non-lawyers like asset managers, bankers, and tax professionals.
Improving task coverage and sample diversity with an emphasis on building datasets that can be used not only for evaluation but for improving models through fine-tuning and training.

kp.k: Snapshot differences and incomplete auditing limit corpus-wide conclusions
kp.d: The document’s reproducibility note distinguishes the May announcement’s 1,250 tasks and more than 75,000 criteria from pinned July 13 repository documentation reporting 1,660 tasks and approximately 101,000 criteria. The Git tree at that commit instead contained 1,749 task.json paths and 14,061 document-file paths. These counts describe different records of an evolving benchmark and must not be substituted for one another; only selected repository materials and a representative task were inspected, not the full matter corpus.
qs: The pinned July 13 repository documentation described 1,660 tasks and approximately 101,000 criteria, while the Git tree at that commit contained 1,749 `task.json` paths and 14,061 document-file paths.
These are different snapshots of an explicitly evolving benchmark, not interchangeable counts.
The complete 14,061-file matter corpus was not acquired or audited.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Harvey's authors present legal agents as enabling selective delegation of legal tasks, with lawyers shifting toward delegation and review rather than being removed from the workflow.
pts.d: Niko Grupen, Gabe Pereyra and Julio Pereyra argue that LAB can identify which tasks agents can perform fully, partly or not at all, helping firms target AI investment and accelerate client value. They envisage lawyers delegating suitable work to agents and reviewing the resulting work product, while retaining substantial human involvement where agents struggle. They also claim that a shared public benchmark can accelerate agent development, not merely measure it. These are deployment and research claims, not reported findings about workforce displacement, realised cost savings or autonomous delivery of legal services. Their reference to a 'high-leverage delegate and review pattern' describes a workflow, not a quantified associate-to-partner staffing ratio.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors ground their claims in benchmark design, experience building legal agents and an analogy with coding agents; the supplied announcement does not report model scores or measured deployment returns.
pts.d: Harvey cites a year of legal-agent development and describes 1,250 tasks across 24 practice areas, assessed using more than 75,000 expert-written criteria. Tasks originate in real client matters and are structured around associate-style assignments, closed-universe matter files and reviewable deliverables. The fictional acquisition example illustrates task complexity rather than an observed client outcome. All-pass grading operationalises the authors' view that omitted legal issues can make a deliverable materially incomplete. This is benchmarking through expert rubrics, potentially applied by an LLM judge, rather than evidence that human verification before reliance is unnecessary. The authors also invoke their engineering team's experience and coding benchmarks as an analogy for making progress visible. They report existing internal and research-community use of LAB, but provide no quantified research gains. The supplied text says results are forthcoming; its holding note references a separate results post without reproducing those results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The May 6, 2026 announcement describes an initial, evolving benchmark, with baseline results expected within weeks and wider coverage planned over time.
pts.d: The authors position selective delegation as a present deployment opportunity conditional on task-specific capability and appropriate lawyer involvement; they do not specify a date for general legal-task autonomy. At launch, no leaderboard is published, and baseline results and submission-normalisation standards remain forthcoming. The initial coverage is explicitly incomplete, with expansion planned across law-firm practices, in-house work and adjacent professional domains. The document's reproducibility note distinguishes the announcement's 1,250 tasks from later repository documentation reporting 1,660 tasks and approximately 101,000 criteria, and from 1,749 task.json paths in the pinned Git tree. Those are different snapshots, not interchangeable evidence of capability. The note also states that the full matter corpus was not acquired or audited.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate focus is large law firms, their lawyers and clients, alongside the researchers and technology builders developing legal agents.
pts.d: Large firms are the intended users of benchmark information for investment and workflow-delegation decisions. Associate-style tasks are the principal work being modelled, while partners and clients supply the review standards that the rubrics seek to emulate. Lawyers remain responsible for review and for execution where agents are less capable; clients are the intended beneficiaries of faster value delivery. Model providers, agent builders, legal technologists and researchers receive a shared testing and development resource. In-house counsel, asset managers, bankers and tax professionals are prospective beneficiaries of planned expansion rather than demonstrated coverage in the initial release. The source makes no concrete claim about changes in associate headcount, billing models or access to justice.
